It is the Moroccan wall in Western Sahara

he Moroccan Wall, also known as the Berm of Western Sahara, is a 2,700-kilometer-long fortification made of sand and stone that snakes through the desert. Constructed by Morocco starting in the 1980s, it serves as a massive military barrier separating the Moroccan-controlled "Southern Provinces" from the territory held by the Polisario Front.

It is estimated to be surrounded by the longest continuous minefield on Earth, with millions of landmines buried along its length.
Despite being made almost entirely of desert sand and rocks, the structure is so massive that it is clearly visible from space.
The wall is actually a series of six distinct defensive lines built over several years, each one pushing further into the desert to consolidate territory.

6. On a map it appears unremarkable — an elongated body of water sprawling across a Central Asian steppe, too large for one glance to take in. But beneath its surface lies a hydrological oddity that has puzzled scientists. One half of this lake sustains freshwater ecosystems. The other is decidedly saline — saltwater home to a different set of organisms entirely. The two halves share the same basin but are kept from fully blending by a narrow natural strait, a subtle underwater threshold that has maintained the chemical divide for centuries. No other lake of comparable size is known to exhibit this split character so distinctly.
